nodes.title: Risk
nodes.text: The risk of an estimator $\hat{y}$ on the estimation problem $(P, y, \ell')$ at $\theta \in \Theta$ is $r^P_\theta(\hat{y}) = (\hat{y} \circ P)(\theta)\left[z \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right]$~.

nodes.title: Bayesian risk
nodes.text: The Bayesian risk of an estimator $\hat{y}$ on $(P, y, \ell')$ for a prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ is $R^P_\pi(\hat{y}) = \pi\left[\theta \mapsto r^P_\theta(\hat{y})\right]$~. It can also be expanded as $R^P_\pi(\hat{y}) = (\pi \otimes (\hat{y} \circ P))\left[ (\theta, z) \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z) \right]$~.

nodes.title: Bayes risk
nodes.text: The Bayes risk of $(P, y, \ell')$ for prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ is $\mathcal R^P_\pi = \inf_{\hat{y} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z} R^P_\pi(\hat{y})$~, where the infimum is over Markov kernels. The Bayes risk of $(P, y, \ell')$ is $\mathcal R^*_B = \sup_{\pi \in \mathcal P(\Theta)} \mathcal R^P_\pi \: .$

nodes.title: Bayes estimator
nodes.text: An estimator $\hat{y}$ is said to be a Bayes estimator for a prior $\pi \in \mathcal P(\Theta)$ if $R^P_\pi(\hat{y}) = \mathcal R^P_\pi$.

nodes.title: Minimax risk
nodes.text: The minimax risk of $(P, y, \ell')$ is $\mathcal R^* = \inf_{\hat{y} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z} \sup_{\theta \in \Theta} r^P_\theta(\hat{y})$~.
$\mathcal R_B^* \le \mathcal R^*$.

The Bayes risk of a prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ on $(P, y, \ell')$ with $P$ a Markov kernel satisfies \begin{align*} \mathcal R^P_\pi \le \inf_{z \in \mathcal Z} \pi\left[ \theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z) \right] \: . \end{align*}

The Bayes risk of a prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ on $(P, y, \ell')$ with $P$ a constant Markov kernel is \begin{align*} \mathcal R^P_\pi = \inf_{z \in \mathcal Z} \pi\left[\theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \: . \end{align*} In particular, it does not depend on $P$.

nodes.title: Data-processing inequality
nodes.text: For $P : \Theta \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ and $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X'$ a Markov kernel, $\mathcal R^{\kappa \circ P}_\pi \ge \mathcal R^{P}_\pi$ (where the estimation problems differ only in the kernel).
For $P : \Theta \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ and $\kappa : \Theta \times \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X'$ a Markov kernel, $\mathcal R^{P \otimes \kappa}_\pi \le \mathcal R^{P}_\pi$~.

For $P : \Theta \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ and $\kappa : \Theta \times \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X'$ a Markov kernel, $\mathcal R^{P \otimes \kappa}_\pi \le \mathcal R^{(P \otimes \kappa)_{\mathcal X'}}_\pi$~, in which $(P \otimes \kappa)_{\mathcal X'} : \mathcal \Theta \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X'$ is the kernel obtained by marginalizing over $\mathcal X$ in the output of $P \otimes \kappa$~.
The Bayes risk $\mathcal R_\pi^P$ is concave in $P : \Theta \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$~.

The Bayesian risk of a Markov kernel $\hat{y} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$ with respect to a prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ on $(P, y, \ell')$ satisfies \begin{align*} R^P_\pi(\hat{y}) = ((P_\pi^\dagger \times \hat{y}) \circ P \circ \pi)\left[(\theta, z) \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \: , \end{align*} whenever the Bayesian inverse $P_\pi^\dagger$ of $P$ with respect to $\pi$ exists (Definition~\ref{def:bayesInv}).

The Bayesian risk of a Markov kernel $\hat{y} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$ with respect to a prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ on $(P, y, \ell')$ satisfies \begin{align*} R^P_\pi(\hat{y}) \ge (P \circ \pi)\left[x \mapsto \inf_{z \in \mathcal Z} P_\pi^\dagger(x) \left[\theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right]\right] \: . \end{align*}

nodes.title: Generalized Bayes estimator
nodes.text: The generalized Bayes estimator for prior $\pi \in \mathcal P(\Theta)$ on $(P, y, \ell')$ is the deterministic estimator $\mathcal X \to \mathcal Z$ given by \begin{align*} x \mapsto \arg\min_z P_\pi^\dagger(x)\left[\theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \: , \end{align*} if there exists such a measurable argmin.

The Bayesian risk of the generalized Bayes estimator $\hat{y}_B$ is \begin{align*} R^P_\pi(\hat{y}_B) = (P \circ \pi)\left[x \mapsto \inf_{z \in \mathcal Z} P_\pi^\dagger(x) \left[\theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right]\right] \: . \end{align*}

When the generalized Bayes estimator is well defined, it is a Bayes estimator. The value of the Bayes risk with respect to the prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ is then \begin{align*} \mathcal R^P_\pi = (P \circ \pi)\left[x \mapsto \inf_{z \in \mathcal Z} P_\pi^\dagger(x) \left[\theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right]\right] \: . \end{align*}

When the generalized Bayes estimator is well defined, the Bayes risk with respect to the prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ is \begin{align*} \mathcal R^P_\pi = (P \circ \pi)\left[x \mapsto \inf_{z \in \mathcal Z} \pi \left[\theta \mapsto \frac{d P_\theta}{d (P \circ \pi)}(x) \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right]\right] \: . \end{align*}

When the generalized Bayes estimator is well defined, the Bayes risk with respect to the prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ for $\mathcal Y = \mathcal Z = \Theta$, $y = \mathrm{id}$ and $\ell' = \mathbb{I}\{\theta \ne z\}$ is \begin{align*} \mathcal R^P_\pi = (P \circ \pi)[1] - (P \circ \pi)\left[x \mapsto \sup_{z \in \mathcal Z} P_\pi^\dagger(x) \{z\}\right] \: . \end{align*}

When the generalized Bayes estimator is well defined, the Bayes risk with respect to the prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ for $\mathcal Y = \mathcal Z = \Theta$, $y = \mathrm{id}$ and $\ell' = \mathbb{I}\{\theta \ne z\}$ is \begin{align*} \mathcal R^P_\pi = (P \circ \pi)[1] - (P \circ \pi)\left[x \mapsto \sup_{z \in \mathcal Z} \frac{d P_z}{d (P \circ \pi)}(x) \pi\{z\} \right] \: . \end{align*} When $\pi$ is a probability measure and $P$ is a Markov kernel, $(P \circ \pi)[1] = 1$.

The generalized Bayes estimator for prior $\pi \in \mathcal P(\Theta)$ on the estimation problem defined by $\mathcal Y = \mathcal Z = \Theta$, $y = \mathrm{id}$ and $\ell' = \mathbb{I}\{\theta \ne z\}$ is \begin{align*} x \mapsto \arg\max_z \left( \pi\{z\} \frac{d P_z}{d (P \circ \pi)}(x) \right) \: . \end{align*}

Suppose that $\Theta$ is finite and let $\xi \in \mathcal P(\Theta)$. The Bayes risk with respect to the prior $\pi \in \mathcal P(\Theta)$ for $\mathcal Y = \mathcal Z = \Theta$, $y = \mathrm{id}$, $P$ a Markov kernel and $\ell' = \mathbb{I}\{\theta \ne z\}$ satisfies \begin{align*} \mathcal R^P_\pi \le 1 - \left(\prod_{\theta \in \Theta} \pi_\theta^{\xi_\theta}\right) (P \circ \pi)\left[x \mapsto \prod_{\theta \in \Theta} \left(\frac{d P_\theta}{d (P \circ \pi)}(x)\right)^{\xi_\theta} \right] \: . \end{align*}

The Bayes risk increase $I^P_{\pi}(\kappa)$ of a kernel $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X'$ with respect to the estimation problem $(P, y, \ell')$ and the prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ is the difference of the Bayes risk of $(\kappa \circ P, y, \ell')$ and that of $(P, y, \ell')$. That is, \begin{align*} I^P_{\pi}(\kappa) &= \mathcal R^{\kappa \circ P}_\pi - \mathcal R^P_\pi \\ &= \inf_{\hat{y} : \mathcal X' \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z} (\pi \otimes (\hat{y} \circ \kappa \circ P))\left[(\theta, z) \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] - \inf_{\hat{y} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z} (\pi \otimes (\hat{y} \circ P))\left[(\theta, z) \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \: . \end{align*}
For $\kappa$ a Markov kernel, $I^P_\pi(\kappa) \ge 0$~.

For $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X'$ and $\eta : \mathcal X' \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X''$ two Markov kernels, $I^P_\pi(\eta \circ \kappa) = I^P_\pi(\kappa) + I^{\kappa \circ P}_\pi(\eta)$~.

The Bayesian inverse of a kernel $P : \{0,1\} \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ with respect to a prior $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$ is $P_\xi^\dagger(x) = \left(\xi_0\frac{d P(0)}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x), \xi_1\frac{d P(1)}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x)\right)$ (almost surely w.r.t. $P \circ \xi = \xi_0 P(0) + \xi_1 P(1)$).

nodes.title: Divergence
nodes.text: A divergence between measures is a function $D$ which for any measurable space $\mathcal X$ and any two measures $\mu, \nu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$, returns a value $D(\mu, \nu) \in \mathbb{R} \cup \{+\infty\}$.

nodes.text: Let $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a convex function. For $a > 0$ and $f$ a convex function, the curvature measure of $af$ is $\gamma_{af} = a \gamma_f$~.

Let $f,g$ be two convex functions whose effective domains have the same endpoints $a \le b$, and such that the right derivatives $f'_+$ and $g'_+$ either both tend to $-\infty$ at $a$ or both have a finite limit at $a$. Then the curvature measure of $f+g$ is $\gamma_{f+g} = \gamma_f + \gamma_g$~. In particular, this holds for $f,g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ two convex functions.

Let $\mu, 
u$ be two finite measures on $\mathcal X$ and $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ two Markov kernels. Then $\KL(\mu \otimes \kappa, 
u \otimes \eta) = \KL(\mu, 
u) + \KL(\mu \otimes \kappa, \mu \otimes \eta)$.

nodes.title: Chain rule, kernel version
nodes.text:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be two finite measures on $\mathcal X$ and $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ two Markov kernels, with either $\mathcal X$ countable or $\mathcal{Y}$ countably generated. Then $\KL(\mu \otimes \kappa, 
u \otimes \eta) = \KL(\mu, 
u) + \KL(\kappa, \eta \mid \mu)$.

nodes.title: Chain rule, with Bayesian inverse
nodes.text:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be two finite measures on $\mathcal X$ and $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ two Markov kernels with Bayesian inverses $\kappa_\mu^\dagger$ and $\eta_
u^\dagger$. Then  egin{align*} \KL(\mu \otimes \kappa, 
u \otimes \eta) = \KL(\kappa \circ \mu, \eta \circ 
u) + \KL(\kappa_\mu^\dagger, \eta_
u^\dagger \mid \kappa \circ \mu) \: . \end{align*}

nodes.title: Chain rule, product version
nodes.text:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be two finite measures on $\mathcal X 	imes \mathcal Y$, where $\mathcal Y$ is standard Borel. Then $\KL(\mu, 
u) = \KL(\mu_X, 
u_X) + \KL(\mu_{Y|X}, 
u_{Y|X} \mid \mu_X)$.

Let $\mu_1, 
u_1$ be finite measures on $\mathcal X$ and $\mu_2, 
u_2$ probability measures on $\mathcal{Y}$. Then $$\KL(\mu_1	imes \mu_2, 
u_1 	imes 
u_2) = \KL(\mu_1, 
u_1) + \KL(\mu_2, 
u_2) \mu_1 (\mathcal X) \: .$$

nodes.title: Tensorization
nodes.text:
For $\mu_1$ a probability measure on $\mathcal X$, $
u_1$ a finite measure on $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mu_2, 
u_2$ two probability measures on $\mathcal Y$,  egin{align*} \KL(\mu_1 	imes \mu_2, 
u_1 	imes 
u_2) = \KL(\mu_1, 
u_1) + \KL(\mu_2 	imes 
u_2) \: . \end{align*}

nodes.text:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be two measures and $E$ an event. Let $\mu_{|E}$ be the measure defined by $\mu_{|E}(A) =  rac{\mu(A \cap E)}{\mu(E)}$ and define $
u_{|E}$, $\mu_{| E^c}$ and $
u_{| E^c}$ similarly. Let $\kl(p,q) = p\log rac{p}{q} + (1-p)\log rac{1-p}{1-q}$ be the Kullback-Leibler divergence between Bernoulli distributions with means $p$ and $q$. Then  egin{align*} \KL(\mu, 
u) \ge \kl(\mu(E), 
u(E)) + \mu(E) \KL(\mu_{|E}, 
u_{|E}) + \mu(E^c) \KL(\mu_{|E^c}, 
u_{|E^c}) \: . \end{align*}

Let $\mu, 
u$ be two measures and $E$ an event. Then $\mu(E)\log rac{\mu(E)}{
u(E)} \le \mu\left[\mathbb{I}(E)\log  rac{d \mu}{d 
u}ight]$ .

nodes.title: Hellinger $\alpha$-divergence
nodes.text:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be two measures on $\mathcal X$. The Hellinger divergence of order $\alpha \in [0,+\infty)$ between $\mu$ and $
u$ is  egin{align*} \He_\alpha(\mu, 
u) = \left\{  egin{array}{ll} 
u \{x \mid  rac{d\mu}{d
u} (x) = 0\} & 	ext{for } \alpha = 0 \ \KL(\mu, 
u) & 	ext{for } \alpha = 1 \ D_{f_\alpha}(\mu, 
u) & 	ext{for } \alpha \in (0,+\infty)  ackslash \{1\} \end{array}ight. \end{align*} with $f_\alpha : x \mapsto  rac{x^{\alpha} - 1}{\alpha - 1}$.
For $\alpha \in [0, 1)$ and finite measures $\mu, \nu$, $\He_\alpha(\mu, \nu) < \infty$.

For $\alpha \in (0,1)\cup(1, \infty)$, $\mu$ a finite measure and $
u$ a probability measure, if $\He_\alpha(\mu, 
u) < \infty$ then  egin{align*} \He_\alpha(\mu, 
u) =  rac{1}{\alpha - 1} \left( \int_x \left( rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)ight)^\alpha \partial 
u - 1 ight) \: . \end{align*}

For $\alpha \in (0,1)\cup(1, \infty)$, $\mu, 
u$ two sigma-finite measures,  egin{align*} \int_x \left( rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)ight)^\alpha \partial 
u = \int_x \left( rac{d 
u}{d \mu}(x)ight)^{1 - \alpha} \partial \mu \: . \end{align*}

For $\alpha \in (0, 1)$ and finite measures $\mu, 
u$, $(1 - \alpha) \He_\alpha(\mu, 
u) = \alpha \He_{1 - \alpha}(
u, \mu)$.

nodes.title: Conditional Hellinger $\alpha$-divergence
nodes.text: Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\mathcal X$ and $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be two kernels. The conditional Hellinger divergence of order $\alpha \in (0,+\infty) \backslash \{1\}$ between $\kappa$ and $\eta$ conditionally to $\mu$ is \begin{align*} \He_\alpha(\kappa, \eta \mid \mu) = D_{f_\alpha}(\kappa, \eta \mid \mu) \: , \end{align*} for $f_\alpha : x \mapsto \frac{x^{\alpha} - 1}{\alpha - 1}$.

nodes.title: Data-processing
nodes.text:
Let $\alpha > 0$, $\mu, 
u$ be two finite measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be a Markov kernel. Then $\He_\alpha(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) \le \He_\alpha(\mu, 
u)$.
Let $\mu, \nu$ be two probability measures. Then $\He_\alpha(\mu, \nu) \ge 0$.
$(\mu, \nu) \mapsto \He_\alpha(\mu, \nu)$ is convex.

nodes.title: Rényi divergence
nodes.text:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be two finite measures on $\mathcal X$. The Rényi divergence of order $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ between $\mu$ and $
u$ is  egin{align*} R_\alpha(\mu, 
u) = \left\{  egin{array}{ll} - \log \left( 
u\{x \mid  rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x) > 0\} / 
u(\mathcal X) ight) & 	ext{for } \alpha = 0 \ \KL(\mu / \mu(\mathcal X), 
u / 
u(\mathcal X)) & 	ext{for } \alpha = 1 \  rac{1}{\alpha - 1} \log \left(  rac{(1 - \alpha) 
u(\mathcal X) + \alpha \mu(\mathcal X) + (\alpha - 1) \He_\alpha(\mu, 
u)}{\mu(\mathcal X)^\alpha 
u(\mathcal X)^{1 - \alpha}} ight) & 	ext{for } \alpha 
otin \{0, 1\} \end{array}ight. \end{align*} It is the Rényi divergence of the normalized measures $\mu / \mu(\mathcal X)$ and $
u / 
u(\mathcal X)$. For $\alpha 
otin \{0, 1\}$, the numerator inside the logarithm is $\int \left( rac{d \mu}{d 
u}ight)^\alpha d
u$.

For $\mu$ a sigma-finite measure and $
u$ a finite measure \[R_0(\mu, 
u) = - \log(
u\{x \mid  rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x) > 0\}) \: .\]

For $\alpha \in [0, 1)$ and finite measures $\mu, 
u$, \[R_\alpha(\mu, 
u) = \infty \iff \mu \perp 
u \: .\]

For $\alpha \in (0,1)\cup(1, \infty)$ and finite measures $\mu, 
u$, if $\left( rac{d \mu}{d 
u}ight)^\alpha$ is integrable with respect to $
u$ and $\mu \ll 
u$ then  egin{align*} R_\alpha(\mu, 
u) =  rac{1}{\alpha - 1} \log \int_x \left( rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)ight)^\alpha \partial 
u \: . \end{align*}

For $\alpha \in (0,1)\cup(1, \infty)$ and finite measures $\mu, 
u$, if $\left( rac{d \mu}{d 
u}ight)^\alpha$ is integrable with respect to $
u$ and $\mu \ll 
u$ then  egin{align*} R_\alpha(\mu, 
u) =  rac{1}{\alpha - 1} \log \int_x \left( rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)ight)^{\alpha - 1} \partial \mu \: . \end{align*}

For $\alpha \in (0, 1)$ and finite measures $\mu, 
u$ with $\mu(\mathcal X) = 
u(\mathcal X)$, \[(1 - \alpha) R_\alpha(\mu, 
u) = \alpha R_{1 - \alpha}(
u, \mu) \: .\]

The cumulant generating function of $\log rac{d\mu}{d
u}$ under $
u$ is $\alpha \mapsto (\alpha - 1) R_\alpha(\mu, 
u)$.

Set $\alpha > 0$. If $R_{1+\alpha}(\mu, 
u) < \infty$, the cumulant generating function of $\log rac{d\mu}{d
u}$ under $\mu$ has value $\alpha R_{1+\alpha}(\mu, 
u)$ at $\alpha$.

nodes.title: Conditional Rényi divergence
nodes.text: Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\mathcal X$ and $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be two kernels. The conditional Rényi divergence of order $\alpha \in (0,+\infty) \backslash \{1\}$ between $\kappa$ and $\eta$ conditionally to $\mu$ is \begin{align*} R_\alpha(\kappa, \eta \mid \mu) =\frac{1}{\alpha - 1} \log (1 + (\alpha - 1) \He_\alpha(\kappa, \eta \mid \mu)) \: . \end{align*}

nodes.title: Data-processing
nodes.text:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be two finite measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be a Markov kernel. Then $R_\alpha(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) \le R_\alpha(\mu, 
u)$.

Let $\mu, 
u$ be two measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $E$ be an event. Let $\mu_E$ and $
u_E$ be the two Bernoulli distributions with respective means $\mu(E)$ and $
u(E)$. Then $R_\alpha(\mu, 
u) \ge R_\alpha(\mu_E, 
u_E)$.

Let $\mu, 
u$ be two finite measures. $R_0(\mu, 
u) = \lim_{\alpha \downarrow 0} R_\alpha(\mu, 
u)$.

Let $\mu, 
u$ be two finite measures. $R_1(\mu, 
u) = \lim_{\alpha \uparrow 1} R_\alpha(\mu, 
u)$.

Let $\mu, 
u$ be two finite measures such that there exists $\alpha > 1$ with $R_\alpha(\mu, 
u)$ finite. Then $R_1(\mu, 
u) = \lim_{\alpha \downarrow 1} R_\alpha(\mu, 
u)$.
Let $\mu, \nu$ be two finite measures. Then $\alpha \mapsto R_\alpha(\mu, \nu)$ is nondecreasing on $[0, + \infty)$.

Let $\mu, 
u$ be two finite measures. Then $\alpha \mapsto R_\alpha(\mu, 
u)$ is continuous on $[0, 1]$ and on $[0, \sup \{\alpha \mid R_\alpha(\mu, 
u) < \infty\})$.

Let $\mu, 
u$ be two measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $\alpha \in (0, +\infty)  ackslash \{1\}$. Let $p =  rac{d \mu}{d (\mu + 
u)}$ and $q =  rac{d 
u}{d (\mu + 
u)}$. We define a measure $\mu^{(\alpha, 
u)}$, absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu + 
u$ with density  egin{align*}  rac{d \mu^{(\alpha, 
u)}}{d (\mu + 
u)} = p^\alpha q^{1 - \alpha} e^{-(\alpha - 1)R_\alpha(\mu, 
u)} \: . \end{align*}

For $\alpha \in (0,1)$, $\mu^{(\alpha, 
u)} \ll \mu$ and $\mu^{(\alpha, 
u)} \ll 
u$.

$ rac{d \mu^{(\alpha, 
u)}}{d 
u} = \left( rac{d\mu}{d
u}ight)^\alpha e^{-(\alpha - 1) R_\alpha(\mu, 
u)}$~, $
u$-a.e., and $ rac{d \mu^{(\alpha, 
u)}}{d \mu} = \left( rac{d
u}{d\mu}ight)^{1 - \alpha} e^{-(\alpha - 1) R_\alpha(\mu, 
u)}$~, $\mu$-a.e..

Let $\mu, 
u, \xi$ be three measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $\alpha \in (0, 1)$. Then  egin{align*} \KL(\xi, \mu^{(\alpha, 
u)}) = \alpha \KL(\xi, \mu) + (1 - \alpha)\KL(\xi, 
u) - (1 - \alpha) R_\alpha(\mu, 
u) \: . \end{align*}

Let $\mu, 
u, \xi$ be three measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $\alpha \in (0, 1)$. Then  egin{align*} (1 - \alpha) R_\alpha(\mu, 
u) = \alpha \KL(\mu^{(\alpha, 
u)}, \mu) + (1 - \alpha)\KL(\mu^{(\alpha, 
u)}, 
u) \: . \end{align*}

Let $\mu, 
u$ be two probability measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $\alpha \in (0, 1)$. Then  egin{align*} (1 - \alpha) R_\alpha(\mu, 
u) = \inf_{\xi \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)}\left( \alpha \KL(\xi, \mu) + (1 - \alpha)\KL(\xi, 
u) ight) \: . \end{align*} The infimum is attained at $\xi = \mu^{(\alpha, 
u)}$.

Let $\mu, 
u \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ and let $\alpha \in (0, 1)$. Let $\pi_\alpha = (\alpha, 1 - \alpha) \in \mathcal P(\{0,1\})$ and let $P : \{0,1\} ightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ be the kernel with $P(0) = \mu$ and $P(1) = 
u$. Then  egin{align*} (1 - \alpha) R_\alpha(\mu, 
u) = \inf_{\xi \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)} \KL\left( \pi_\alpha 	imes \xi, \pi_\alpha \otimes P ight) \: . \end{align*} The infimum is attained at $\xi = \mu^{(\alpha, 
u)}$.

nodes.title: Chain rule
nodes.text:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be two measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be two Markov kernels. Then $R_\alpha(\mu \otimes \kappa, 
u \otimes \eta) = R_\alpha(\mu, 
u) + R_\alpha(\kappa, \eta \mid \mu^{(\alpha, 
u)})$.

nodes.title: Chain rule, with Bayesian inverse
nodes.text:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be two finite measures on $\mathcal X$ and $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ two Markov kernels with Bayesian inverses $\kappa_\mu^\dagger$ and $\eta_
u^\dagger$. Then  egin{align*} R_\alpha(\mu \otimes \kappa, 
u \otimes \eta) = R_\alpha(\kappa \circ \mu, \eta \circ 
u) + R_\alpha(\kappa_\mu^\dagger, \eta_
u^\dagger \mid (\kappa \circ \mu)^{(\alpha, \eta \circ 
u)}) \: . \end{align*}

Let $\mu, 
u \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ and $\xi, \lambda \in \mathcal P(\mathcal Y)$. Then $R_\alpha(\mu 	imes \xi, 
u 	imes \lambda) = R_\alpha(\mu, 
u) + R_\alpha(\xi, \lambda)$.

nodes.title: Tensorization - finite product
nodes.text:
Let $I$ be a finite index set. Let $(\mu_i)_{i \in I}, (
u_i)_{i \in I}$ be probability measures on measurable spaces $(\mathcal X_i)_{i \in I}$. Then $R_\alpha (\prod_{i \in I} \mu_i, \prod_{i \in I} 
u_i) = \sum_{i \in I} R_\alpha(\mu_i, 
u_i)$.

Let $\mu, 
u$ be two probability measures on $\mathcal X$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and write $\mu^{\otimes n}$ for the product measure on $\mathcal X^n$ of $n$ times $\mu$. Then $R_\alpha(\mu^{\otimes n}, 
u^{\otimes n}) = n R_\alpha(\mu, 
u)$.

nodes.title: Tensorization - countable product
nodes.text:
Let $I$ be a countable index set. Let $(\mu_i)_{i \in I}, (
u_i)_{i \in I}$ be probability measures on measurable spaces $(\mathcal X_i)_{i \in I}$. Then $R_\alpha (\prod_{i \in I} \mu_i, \prod_{i \in I} 
u_i) = \sum_{i \in I} R_\alpha(\mu_i, 
u_i)$.

nodes.title: Squared Hellinger distance
nodes.text:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be two measures. The squared Hellinger distance between $\mu$ and $
u$ is  egin{align*} \Hsq(\mu, 
u) = D_f(\mu, 
u) \quad 	ext{with } f: x \mapsto  rac{1}{2}\left( 1 - \sqrt{x} ight)^2 \: . \end{align*}

nodes.title: Hellinger and Rényi
nodes.text:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be two probability measures. Then $R_{1/2}(\mu, 
u) = -2\log(1 - \Hsq(\mu, 
u))$.

Let $\mu, 
u$ be two probability measures. Then $2 \Hsq(\mu, 
u) \le R_{1/2}(\mu, 
u)$.

Let $\mu, 
u$ be two probability measures. Then $\Hsq(\mu, 
u) \le \TV(\mu, 
u)$.

Let $\mu, 
u$ be two probability measures. Then $\TV(\mu, 
u) \le \sqrt{\Hsq(\mu, 
u)(2 - \Hsq(\mu, 
u))}$.

Let $\mu, 
u$ be two probability measures. Then  egin{align*}  rac{1}{2}(1 - \Hsq(\mu, 
u))^2 \le 1 - \TV(\mu, 
u) -  rac{1}{2}(1 - \TV(\mu, 
u))^2 \: . \end{align*}

Let $\mu, 
u$ be two probability measures. Then  egin{align*} 1 - \sqrt{1 - (1 - \Hsq(\mu, 
u))^2} \le 1 - \TV(\mu, 
u) \le 1 - \Hsq(\mu, 
u) \: . \end{align*}

Let $\mu, 
u$ be two probability measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and $\mu^{\otimes n}, 
u^{\otimes n}$ be their product measures on $\mathcal X^n$. Then  egin{align*}  rac{1}{2}e^{-n R_{1/2}(\mu, 
u)} \le 1 - \sqrt{1 - e^{-n R_{1/2}(\mu, 
u)}} \le 1 - \TV(\mu^{\otimes n}, 
u^{\otimes n}) \le e^{- rac{1}{2} n R_{1/2}(\mu, 
u)} \: . \end{align*}

nodes.title: Chernoff divergence
nodes.text:
The Chernoff divergence of order $\alpha > 0$ between two measures $\mu$ and $
u$ on $\mathcal X$ is  egin{align*} C_\alpha(\mu, 
u) = \inf_{\xi \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)}\max\{R_\alpha(\xi, \mu), R_\alpha(\xi, 
u)\} \: . \end{align*}
$C_1(\mu, \nu) = \inf_{\xi \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)}\max\{\KL(\xi, \mu), \KL(\xi, \nu)\}$ .

nodes.title: Symmetry
nodes.text: $C_\alpha(\mu, \nu) = C_\alpha(\nu, \mu)$.

nodes.title: Monotonicity
nodes.text: The function $\alpha \mapsto C_\alpha(\mu, \nu)$ is monotone.
\begin{align*} C_1(\mu, \nu) = \max_{\alpha\in [0,1]} (1 - \alpha)R_\alpha(\mu, \nu) \: . \end{align*}

nodes.title: Jensen-Shannon divergence
nodes.text:
The Jensen-Shannon divergence indexed by $\alpha \in (0,1)$ between two measures $\mu$ and $
u$ is  egin{align*} \JS_\alpha(\mu, 
u) = \alpha \KL(\mu, \alpha \mu + (1 - \alpha)
u) + (1 - \alpha) \KL(
u, \alpha \mu + (1 - \alpha)
u) \: . \end{align*}

Let $\mu, 
u \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ and let $\alpha \in (0, 1)$. Let $\pi_\alpha = (\alpha, 1 - \alpha) \in \mathcal P(\{0,1\})$ and let $P : \{0,1\} ightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ be the kernel with $P(0) = \mu$ and $P(1) = 
u$. Then  egin{align*} \JS_\alpha(\mu, 
u) = \KL(\pi_\alpha \otimes P, \pi_\alpha 	imes (P \circ \pi_\alpha)) \: . \end{align*}
$\JS_\alpha$ is an $f$-divergence for $f(x) = \alpha x \log(x) - (\alpha x + 1 - \alpha) \log (\alpha x + 1 - \alpha)$~.

For $\alpha \in (0,1)$ and $\mu, 
u \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$,  egin{align*} \JS_\alpha(\mu, 
u) = \JS_{1 - \alpha}(
u, \mu) \: . \end{align*}

Let $\mu, 
u \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ and let $\alpha \in (0, 1)$. Then  egin{align*} \JS_\alpha(\mu, 
u) = \inf_{\xi \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)}\left( \alpha \KL(\mu, \xi) + (1 - \alpha)\KL(
u, \xi) ight) \: . \end{align*} The infimum is attained at $\xi = \alpha \mu + (1 - \alpha) 
u$.

Let $\mu, 
u \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ and let $\alpha \in (0, 1)$. Let $\pi_\alpha = (\alpha, 1 - \alpha) \in \mathcal P(\{0,1\})$ and let $P : \{0,1\} ightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ be the kernel with $P(0) = \mu$ and $P(1) = 
u$. Then  egin{align*} \JS_\alpha(\mu, 
u) = \inf_{\xi \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)} \KL\left( \pi_\alpha \otimes P, \pi_\alpha 	imes \xi ight) \: . \end{align*} The infimum is attained at $\xi = \alpha \mu + (1 - \alpha) 
u$.

Let $\mu, 
u$ be two probability measures on $\mathcal X$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and write $\mu^{\otimes n}$ for the product measure on $\mathcal X^n$ of $n$ times $\mu$. Then $\JS_\alpha(\mu^{\otimes n}, 
u^{\otimes n}) \le n \JS_\alpha(\mu, 
u)$.

For $\mu, 
u \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ and $\alpha, \lambda \in (0,1)$~,  egin{align*} \JS_\alpha(\mu, 
u) \le  rac{(1 - \alpha)^{1 - \lambda} \alpha^\lambda}{\lambda^{1 - \lambda} (1 - \lambda)^\lambda} (1 - \lambda)\He_\lambda(\mu, 
u) \: . \end{align*} In particular,  egin{align*} \JS_\alpha(\mu, 
u) &\le \left( rac{1 - \alpha}{\alpha}ight)^{1 - 2 \alpha} (1 - \alpha)\He_\alpha(\mu, 
u) \: , \ \JS_\alpha(\mu, 
u) &\le \alpha \He_{1 - \alpha}(\mu, 
u) \: . \end{align*}

For $\mu, 
u \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ and $\alpha \in (0,1)$, $\lambda \le 1/2$~,  egin{align*} \JS_\alpha(\mu, 
u) &\le \alpha^{1 - \lambda} \He_{1 - \lambda}(\mu, 
u) \: . \end{align*}
The mutual information is, for $\rho \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X \times \mathcal Y)$~, \begin{align*} I(\rho) = \KL(\rho, \rho_X \times \rho_Y) \: . \end{align*}

Let $\kappa : \mathcal Z ightsquigarrow \mathcal X 	imes \mathcal Y$. The conditional mutual information of $\kappa$ with respect to $
u \in \mathcal M(\mathcal Z)$ is  egin{align*} I(\kappa \mid 
u) = \KL(\kappa, \kappa_X 	imes \kappa_Y \mid 
u) \: . \end{align*}

For $\mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ and $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ a Markov kernel, \begin{align*} I(\mu \otimes \kappa) = KL(\mu \otimes \kappa, \mu \times (\kappa \circ \mu)) = KL(\kappa, \kappa \circ \mu \mid \mu) \: , \end{align*} where in the conditional divergence the measure $\kappa \circ \mu$ should be understood as the constant kernel from $\mathcal X$ to $\mathcal Y$ with that value.
$I(\rho_\leftrightarrow) = I(\rho)$~.

Let $\mu, 
u \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ and let $\alpha \in (0, 1)$. Let $\pi_\alpha = (\alpha, 1 - \alpha) \in \mathcal P(\{0,1\})$ and let $P : \{0,1\} ightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ be the kernel with $P(0) = \mu$ and $P(1) = 
u$. Then  egin{align*} I(\pi_\alpha \otimes P) = \JS_\alpha(\mu, 
u) \: . \end{align*}

nodes.title: Data-processing
nodes.text: For $\rho \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X \times \mathcal Y)$, $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X'$ and $\eta : \mathcal Y \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y'$ two Markov kernels, \begin{align*} I((\kappa \parallel \eta) \circ \rho) \le I(\rho) \: . \end{align*}

For $\mu \in \mathcal X$, $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ and $\eta : \mathcal Y \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$ two Markov kernels, \begin{align*} I(\mu \otimes (\eta \circ \kappa)) \le I(\mu \otimes \kappa) \: . \end{align*}

Let $D$ be a divergence between measures. The left $D$-mutual information for a measure $\mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ and a kernel $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ is \begin{align*} I_D^L(\mu, \kappa) = \inf_{\xi \in \mathcal P(\mathcal Y)} D(\mu \times \xi, \mu \otimes \kappa) \: . \end{align*}

Let $D$ be a divergence between measures. The right $D$-mutual information for a measure $\mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ and a kernel $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ is \begin{align*} I_D^R(\mu, \kappa) = \inf_{\xi \in \mathcal P(\mathcal Y)} D(\mu \otimes \kappa, \mu \times \xi) \: . \end{align*}

nodes.title: Measurable space of measures
nodes.text: Let $\mathcal B$ be the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on $\mathbb{R}_{+,\infty}$. Let $\mathcal X$ be a measurable space. For a measurable set $s$ of $\mathcal X$, let $(\mu \mapsto \mu(s))^* \mathcal B$ be the $\sigma$-algebra on $\mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ defined by the comap of the evaluation function at $s$. Then $\mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ is a measurable space with $\sigma$-algebra $\bigsqcup_{s} (\mu \mapsto \mu(s))^* \mathcal B$ where the supremum is over all measurable sets $s$.

Let $\mathcal X, \mathcal Y$ be measurable spaces, and let $f : \mathcal X \to \mathcal M(\mathcal Y)$ such that for all measurable sets $s$ of $\mathcal X$, the function $x \mapsto f(x)(s)$ is measurable. Then $f$ is measurable.

nodes.title: Kernel
nodes.text: Let $\mathcal X, \mathcal Y$ be two measurable spaces. A probability transition kernel (or simply kernel) from $\mathcal X$ to $\mathcal Y$ is a measurable map from $\mathcal X$ to $\mathcal M (\mathcal Y)$, the measurable space of measures on $\mathcal Y$. We write $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ for a kernel $\kappa$ from $\mathcal X$ to $\mathcal Y$.

nodes.title: Deterministic kernel
nodes.text: The deterministic kernel defined by a measurable function $f : \mathcal X \to \mathcal Y$ is the kernel $d_f: \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ defined by $d_f(x) = \delta_{f(x)}$, where for any $y \in \mathcal Y$, $\delta_y$ is the Dirac probability measure at $y$.

Two kernels $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ are equal iff for all measurable functions $f : \mathcal Y \to \mathbb{R}_{+,\infty}$ and all $x \in \mathcal X$, \begin{align*} \int_y f(y) \partial \kappa(x) = \int_y f(y) \partial \eta(x) \: . \end{align*}

nodes.title: Finite kernel
nodes.text: A kernel $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ is said to be finite if there exists $C < +\infty$ such that for all $x \in \mathcal X$, $\kappa(x)(\mathcal Y) \le C$.

nodes.title: Markov kernel
nodes.text: A kernel $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ is said to be a Markov kernel if for all $x \in \mathcal X$, $\kappa(x)$ is a probability measure.

nodes.title: s-finite kernel
nodes.text: A kernel $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ is said to be a s-finite if it is equal to a countable sum of finite kernels.

nodes.title: Composition-product
nodes.text: Let $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ and $\eta : (\mathcal X \times \mathcal Y) \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$ be two s-finite kernels. The composition-product of $\kappa$ and $\eta$ is a kernel $\kappa \otimes \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow (\mathcal Y \times \mathcal Z)$ such that for all measurable functions $f : \mathcal Y \times \mathcal Z \to \mathbb{R}_{+,\infty}$ and $x \in \mathcal X$~, \begin{align*} \int_{y,z} f(y,z) \partial(\kappa \otimes \eta)(x) = \int_y \int_z f(y,z) \partial\eta(x,y) \partial\kappa(x) \: . \end{align*}

nodes.title: Composition-product of a measure and a kernel
nodes.text: Let $\mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ be an s-finite measure and $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be an s-finite kernel. Let $\mathcal U$ be a measurable space with a unique element $u$. Let $\mu_k : \mathcal U \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ be the constant kernel with value $\mu$. The composition-product of $\mu$ and $\kappa$ is the measure on $\mathcal M(\mathcal X \times \mathcal Y)$ defined by $(\mu_k \otimes \kappa) (u)$~.

nodes.title: Composition
nodes.text: Let $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ and $\eta : \mathcal Y \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$ be two kernels. The composition of $\kappa$ and $\eta$ is the kernel $\eta \circ \kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$ such that for all measurable functions $f : \mathcal Z \to \mathbb{R}_{+,\infty}$ and all $x \in \mathcal X$, \begin{align*} \int_z f(z) \partial(\eta \circ \kappa)(x) = \int_y \int_z f(z) \partial\eta(y) \partial\kappa(x) \: . \end{align*}

nodes.title: Product
nodes.text: Let $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ and $\eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$ be two s-finite kernels. The product of $\kappa$ and $\eta$ is the kernel $\kappa \times \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y \times \mathcal Z$ such that for all measurable functions $f : \mathcal Y \times \mathcal Z \to \mathbb{R}_{+,\infty}$ and all $x \in \mathcal X$, \begin{align*} \int_{y,z} f(y,z) \partial(\kappa \times \eta)(x) = \int_y \int_z f(y,z) \partial\eta(x) \partial\kappa(x) \: . \end{align*}

nodes.title: Parallel product
nodes.text: Let $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ and $\eta : \mathcal X' \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y'$ be two s-finite kernels. The parallel product of $\kappa$ and $\eta$ is the kernel $\kappa \parallel \eta : \mathcal X \times \mathcal X' \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y \times \mathcal Y'$ such that for all measurable functions $f : \mathcal Y \times \mathcal Y' \to \mathbb{R}_{+,\infty}$ and all $x \in \mathcal X \times \mathcal X'$, \begin{align*} \int_{y,y'} f(y,y') \partial(\kappa \parallel \eta)(x,x') = \int_y \int_{y'} f(y,y') \partial\eta(x') \partial\kappa(x) \: . \end{align*}

nodes.title: Blackwell sufficiency
nodes.text: We define a partial order on kernels by the following. Let $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ and $\eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$ (with same domain as $\kappa$). Then $\kappa$ is Blackwell sufficient for $\eta$, denoted by $\eta \le_B \kappa$, if there exists a Markov kernel $\xi : \mathcal Y \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$ such that $\eta = \xi \circ \kappa$.

nodes.title: Disintegration in standard Borel spaces
nodes.text: If either $\mathcal X$ is countable of $\mathcal Y$ has a countably generated $\sigma$-algebra, and $\mathcal Z$ is standard Borel, then for every s-finite kernel $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y \times \mathcal Z$, there exists a Markov kernel $\kappa_{Z \mid Y} : \mathcal X \times \mathcal Y \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$ that disintegrates $\kappa$.

For $\mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ and $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$, a Bayesian inverse of $\kappa$ is a Markov kernel $\kappa_\mu^\dagger : \mathcal Y \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ such that $\mu \otimes \kappa = ((\kappa \circ \mu) \otimes \kappa_\mu^\dagger)_\leftrightarrow$ in which $(\cdot)_\leftrightarrow$ denotes swapping the two coordinates. If such an inverse exists it is unique up to a $(\kappa \circ \mu)$-null set, and we talk about \emph{the} Bayesian inverse of $\kappa$ with respect to $\mu$.

nodes.title: Existence of the Bayesian inverse
nodes.text: For $\mathcal X$ standard Borel, $\mu$ and $\kappa$ s-finite, the Bayesian inverse of $\kappa$ with respect to $\mu$ exists and is obtained by disintegration of the measure $\mu \otimes \kappa$ on $\mathcal X \times \mathcal Y$ into a measure $\kappa \circ \mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal Y)$ and a Markov kernel $\kappa_\mu^\dagger : \mathcal Y \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$.

nodes.title: a.e.-uniqueness of the Bayesian inverse
nodes.text: Let $\mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ be a finite measure and let $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be a finite kernel. If $\eta : \mathcal Y \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ is such that $\mu \otimes \kappa = ((\kappa \circ \mu) \otimes \eta)_\leftrightarrow$, then $\eta(y) = \kappa_\mu^\dagger(y)$ for $(\kappa \circ \mu)$-almost all $y$.

For $\mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ s-finite, $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ a Markov kernel and $\kappa_\mu^\dagger$ the Bayesian inverse of $\kappa$ with respect to $\mu$, these objects satisfy the equality $\kappa_\mu^\dagger \circ \kappa \circ \mu = \mu$.

For $\mathcal X$ and $\mathcal Y$ two standard Borel spaces, $\mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ s-finite and $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ a Markov kernel, $(\kappa_\mu^\dagger)_{\kappa \circ \mu}^\dagger = \kappa$ ($\mu$-a.e.).
Let $\mu \in \mathcal M (\mathcal X)$ and let $\textup{id} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ be the identity kernel. Then $\textup{id}_\mu^\dagger = \textup{id}$.

Let $\mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$, $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ and $\eta : \mathcal Y \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$. Then $(\eta \circ \kappa \circ \mu)$-a.e., \begin{align*} (\eta \circ \kappa)_\mu^\dagger = \kappa_{\mu}^\dagger \circ \eta_{\kappa \circ \mu}^\dagger \: . \end{align*}

Let $\mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ and $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ such that $\kappa_\mu^\dagger$ exists and such that $\kappa(x) \ll \kappa \circ \mu$ almost surely. Then for $\mu$-almost all $x$ and $(\kappa \circ \mu)$-almost all $y$, \begin{align*} \frac{d \kappa_\mu^\dagger(y)}{d \mu}(x) = \frac{d \kappa(x)}{d(\kappa \circ \mu)}(y) \: . \end{align*}
